b: Manga artist and illustrator, author of 『とつくにの少女』 (The Girl from the Other Side). Poster-like illustrations of animal-headed figures in two or three flat colours.
reason: Designed colour taken to its most economical: red, black and jade, hard graphic shadow, almost screen-print. Shares the graphic-invention pole (Mika Pikazo, redjuice) but with none of the luminous-girl idiom — a deliberate stretch in subject and palette.

b: Swedish painter and etcher; portraits, bathers on the Dalarna shore and Stockholm night scenes, cut with long parallel etched strokes.
reason: The bravura-line ancestor of Fechin and Nick Alm, and bathers in moving water — the Monks/Mieno interest in figures seen through water, drawn with a needle instead of a brush.

b: American-born painter and printmaker working in London and Venice; the Nocturnes and the Thames and Venice etchings.
reason: Haze and night as the whole subject — the atmosphere side of the collection (Baugh, Mieno) a century earlier, with almost nothing described.

b: American painter and illustrator; watercolours of the Caribbean and the Maine coast, and early wood-engraved illustrations for Harper's Weekly.
reason: Water and weather handled in transparent washes — light on the sea as the subject; also a painter who began as a magazine illustrator.

b: Portrait painter and watercolourist; the plein-air ease that Lipking and Schmid cite.
reason: The source Lipking and Schmid both point back to: alla prima confidence and light on white fabric.

b: Painter and printmaker of the shin-hanga movement; landscapes and night scenes cut and printed under his own supervision.
reason: Printmaking wildcard: lamplit canals and night streets built from flat, graded woodblock colour — atmosphere and light without a figure, from the same country as the hush cluster.

b: Danish painter of grey, near-empty interiors in his Copenhagen apartment at Strandgade 30.
reason: Sprick's 'air doing something' in a room, pushed to silence — the Morimoto hush without the figure.

b: American painter and printmaker in the Impressionist circle; drypoints and colour prints of women and children.
reason: Quiet domestic figures in printmaking — the hush cluster's subject in line and flat colour.

b: Japanese illustrator and character designer; clean linework and soft flat colour, much of it for games and card art.
reason: The Kantoku/深崎暮人 idiom with more air and less rendering — pale line, pale light, figures that sit quietly in the white of the page.

b: Dutch digital illustrator (Lois van Baarle), known for figure studies in saturated, glowing complementary colour.
reason: Luminous illustration from outside the Japanese idiom: backlit figures, water and starlight done as designed colour and flowing shape rather than rendered detail.

b: Japanese illustrator based in New York; brush-and-ink drawing coloured digitally, for book covers, posters and editorial work.
reason: Graphic invention in ink: the energy and designed colour of the Yoneyama/Mika Pikazo pole, but carried by a brush line with ukiyo-e ancestry.

b: Taiwanese-American artist; former comic-cover illustrator turned painter and printmaker, known for flowing, ornamental figure compositions.
reason: Sits on the line between the two tabs: painted on canvas, but with an illustrator's invented colour and ornament — luminous without being photographic.

b: Swedish illustrator and screen-print artist of ruined architecture and science-fiction landscapes.
reason: Wildcard: no figures to speak of, but atmosphere and designed colour at full strength — haze, scale and a strictly limited print palette.

b: Taiwanese-American illustrator of book covers and personal work in flat, patterned colour.
reason: Graphic invention and pattern — cover work with the same designed-colour logic as redjuice and Mika Pikazo, drawn from a different tradition.

b: Japanese illustrator and graphic designer working on advertising, concept art and character design.
reason: Designed colour reduced to two or three flat inks and a lot of white — the graphic-invention pole (Mika Pikazo, redjuice) crossed with poster design.

b: Animal artist from northern Finland who paints dogs as saints, clerics and figures in devotional panels.
reason: Wildcard: staged, theatrical solemnity (the Kamoi/Ferri appetite for performed feeling) transposed onto dogs in the format of religious icons — deadpan, tender and odd.

b: Freelance illustrator and concept artist; gardens, flowers and water painted digitally in high-key, saturated light.
reason: Light and colour carrying the whole picture with the figure small or absent — the loundraw instinct applied to plants and water.

b: Korean-born Norwegian painter, self-taught; figures suspended in dark, smeared grounds, half-dissolved into the paint.
reason: Staged, lit figures against darkness — the Currie/Lorca line — but with the figure literally breaking up into brushwork.

b: Painter from Cluj who paints small figures at leisure among post-socialist buildings and grey-green landscapes; represented Romania at the 2024 Venice Biennale.
reason: Atmosphere and quiet at landscape scale: haze, muted light, small figures — the hush without a close-up face, in a subject the collection had never touched.

b: Brazilian-born painter in Karlsruhe; large close-cropped faces built from broken, glitch-like strokes of oil.
reason: The face seen through something again — here the interference is the brushwork itself, like Mieno's water rebuilt as paint marks.

b: Minneapolis painter of figures in bars, cafés and dressing rooms, set against loosely brushed, near-empty grounds.
reason: Nick Alm's social scenes and Assael's caught-not-posed figures, with more graphic, flattened grounds and fashion-plate poise.

b: Japanese-born painter in the US working in a Renaissance-derived glazing technique; allegorical women with animals, flowers and Japanese folklore.
reason: Theatrical, staged figuration (Lorca, Ferri) crossed with Japanese folk tales — ornament and invented colour in oil.

b: American painter of warm, lamplit interiors, cafés and solitary figures.
reason: Lamplight and interior warmth — the quiet-figure line with amber light instead of Morimoto's grey.

b: Manga artist and illustrator; author of 『とんがり帽子のアトリエ』 (Witch Hat Atelier), serialised in Kodansha's Morning two.
reason: Luminous illustration by way of pen-and-ink: ornamental line and printed-looking colour, closer to golden-age book illustration than to anime rendering.

b: Japanese landscape illustrator (風景画家) working mainly on scenery and backgrounds.
reason: loundraw's atmosphere with the figure almost gone: skies, reflections and station platforms at dusk — light and air as the whole subject.

b: Anime background artist (背景美術) who also paints scenery for pleasure, digitally and in analogue media.
reason: Night reflections and low sun painted by someone whose job is atmosphere — the background-art craft behind the luminous-illustration idiom.

b: American oil painter of mythology, nature and folklore — nymphs, animals and fairy-tale figures in warm, glazed woodland light.
reason: Staged, lit figures in the Lorca/Ferri line, but pastoral rather than dark: folklore theatre in a Rococo palette.

b: Oil painter and educator associated with the Barcelona Academy of Art and Alla Prima Academy; portraits painted directly from life.
reason: Alla prima portraits with visible, confident brushwork — the Schmid/Blokhin handling in the present tense, and a working teacher.

b: Oil painter and charcoal draughtsman working largely in fantasy illustration.
reason: Theatrical figures lit against darkness, painted for fantasy illustration — illustration that is traditional oil and charcoal.

b: Concept artist with three decades in the film industry, and oil painter of science-fiction landscapes.
reason: Wildcard: vast hazy landscapes and tiny figures — atmosphere and scale over portraiture, painted in oil by a film concept artist.

b: Illustrator and screen-printer of houses, trees and lit windows at night.
reason: Printmaking wildcard: night atmosphere from a few flat inks — Whistler's nocturnes as a screen print.

b: Animation artist and illustrator of dreamlike skies and water, drawn without outlines; music-video and jacket work.
reason: The weightless, high-key light of loundraw and 白身魚 at its most distilled — cloud, moon and water in pale blues.

b: Freelance illustrator of book covers, packaging and music videos; art book 『ささめうた』.
reason: Line-led, near-monochrome figures with a few spot colours — graphic restraint (redjuice) crossed with the delicacy of the hush cluster.

b: Background designer and illustrator (背景デザイナー); background art for 電撃文庫『リビルドワールド』 and 文藝春秋『剣樹抄』 among others.
reason: Dense, lamplit cityscapes and towers in haze — atmosphere and light built as architecture, the background craft behind luminous illustration.

b: Japanese artist who paints by hand with brush on paper: small animals, flowers and odd creatures in watercolour and ink.
reason: Traditional illustration with a light, patient brush — quiet like the hush cluster, but botanical, humorous and hand-painted rather than rendered.

b: Illustrator of 『お隣の天使様にいつの間にか駄目人間にされていた件』 and the SNOW MIKU 2020 main visual.
reason: The backlit after-school idiom of カントク and 深崎暮人 — soft rim light, reflections, sunflowers — but with more sky and water around the figure.

b: Japanese illustrator working in a signature mint-and-black palette; prints and character art.
reason: Designed colour held to one palette — the LAM/redjuice discipline of a limited, artificial colour scheme.

b: Japanese illustrator of stylised, flatly coloured character designs.
reason: Graphic invention in character design: flat colour, sharp silhouettes and a lot of white — closer to fashion plates than to rendered anime.

b: Vietnamese-born American painter in Denver; figures, interiors, kitchens, landscapes and flowers in oil, painted from direct observation.
reason: The Schmid/Lipking handling at full strength — shapes, edges and colour doing the work, with the same painterly ease across figures, snow and flowers.

b: American painter of portraits and quiet interiors; figures by windows and in lamplight, painted in oil, and charcoal portrait drawings.
reason: The hush in an American key — a figure alone in a room with one source of light, soft edges and a still, withheld mood.
